headline_hi: कार की अनोखी घूमने वाली सीट
summary_en: Very inspiring news has come from Bengaluru. Here, engineers Naina Padaki and Anand Kutre have done wonderful work. They started a special initiative called 'True Assistive Technology'. Their team has made a swivel seat for cars named 'TurnPlus'. This seat turns ninety degrees towards the door. This makes it very easy to seat any patient in a car. Rashmi Sampath from Bengaluru lives with her sixteen-year-old daughter Deeksha. Deeksha had severe mobility issues, so going out was difficult. With the help of this new seat, they traveled from Bengaluru to Kanyakumari. Throughout this nearly one thousand-kilometer journey, Deeksha remained very comfortable. This technology has helped more than one thousand people across India. Now, going out together has become extremely easy for many families.

lead.title: This Bengaluru Couple’s Swivel Car Seat Has Helped 1000+ People With Disabilities Travel Again
lead.summary: "Earlier, it was very difficult for me," says Bengaluru resident Rashmi Sampath, recalling every family outing with her 16-year-old daughter, Deeksha, who has spinal muscular atrophy. "She weighs 55 kilograms, and lifting her into the car was exhausting. But now, since the seat rotates 90 degrees, it is very comfortable." The difference has been more than convenience. A journey that once demanded careful planning, physical effort, and frequent compromises has become something the family can look forward to. Last year, they drove nearly 1,000 kilometres from Bengaluru to Kanyakumari without the travel itself becoming an obstacle. "She was very comfortable throughout," Rashmi says. "We took just two breaks. She could even sleep on the seat. Earlier, we couldn't have imagined travelling such a long distance like this." For millions of Indians living with disabilities or age-related mobility challenges, the hardest part of a journey often begins before the vehicle even starts moving. Getting into a car can require multiple people, unsafe lifting techniques, or simply deciding that the trip isn't worth the effort. It is this overlooked challenge that Bengaluru-based TRUE Assistive Technology set out to address. Founded by engineers Naina Padaki and Anand Kutre, the company designs assistive mobility solutions, including swivel seats, portable ramps, transfer systems, and wheelchair-accessible vehicle modifications, that make everyday travel safer and more accessible.  TurnPlus rotates towards the car door, making it easier for passengers to get in and out with less physical strain. headline_hi: छात्रों ने घटाया प्लास्टिक का कचरा
summary_en: Schoolchildren across the world are coming forward against plastic pollution. In a school in Singapore, children saw plastic waste in the canteen. There, two thousand children used seventy-two thousand plastic items every year. The students ran a major campaign to stop this problem. They introduced the practice of reusable tiffin boxes. For this brilliant idea, they won first place in the 'Unplastify Challenge'. Four hundred schools from twenty-five countries have joined this global program. Together, around three thousand schoolchildren have saved seventy-two tons of plastic waste. Students in Chile discovered a natural alternative to glittery plastic. Meanwhile, in Costa Rica, children chose natural loofah instead of plastic sponges. Children in Turkey prepared new types of gloves for hospitals. With the wisdom of these young children, our Earth is becoming clean and safe.

lead.title: Teenagers Worldwide Are Tackling the Plastics Crisis
lead.summary: W hen students in Singapore looked around their school cafeteria, they could see a problem shared all over the world: Single-use Styrofoam was ubiquitous. They soon learned that the school’s 2,000 students used 72,000 pieces of Styrofoam and other types of plastic every year. To find a solution, they joined the Unplastify Challenge , a global movement initiated by the Latin American social enterprise Unplastify and funded by the National Geographic Society, a nonprofit that seeks to foster environmental stewardship. What makes the program unique is its audience, design and scope. Teenagers, usually 15 to 16 years old, design and implement solutions to “unplastify” their schools, communities, neighborhoods and homes. In Singapore, the students decided to campaign for multi-use lunch boxes, winning them first place in the Unplastify Challenge 2026, the 12th such event of its kind. A garbage-strewn beach in Bali, Indonesia. Unless effective action is taken, it’s predicted that global plastic production will more than double over the next 15 years. Credit: Mariia Ploshikhina / Shutterstock In the eight years since it began, Unplastify has worked with over 3,000 students at 400 schools in 25 countries, mostly in Latin America, but also in Africa, Asia, North America and Europe. Together these students have come up with over 1,000 strategies, leading efforts to avoid an estimated 72 tons of plastic. In Chile, students have designed a biodegradable alternative to plastic glitter, thus avoiding four kilos of plastic in a single year. In Costa Rica, students have replaced plastic sponges with natural luffa. headline_hi: कंक्रीट की दीवार पर उगेगी हरियाली
headline_en: Greenery will grow on concrete walls
summary_en: Science has made a unique discovery for environmental improvement. Respyre, a new startup from the Netherlands, has created the 'Mosscrete' technology. This is a method to grow moss on concrete walls. This technology was developed through research from Delft University of Technology. In this technology, there is no need to put soil or pipes on walls. Fine moss fibers absorb moisture directly from rain and air. With this, both old and new buildings can be made green. Its testing is underway on eight different buildings in the Netherlands and Belgium. In Kortrijk, Belgium, a wall of four hundred and fifty square meters was made green. Meanwhile, an experiment was conducted on a three hundred square meter wall in Hoofddorp, Netherlands. This invention will make cities' blank walls beautiful without any maintenance. Through this, our cities will be able to become full of clean air and natural greenery.
source: The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News

lead.title: A Dutch startup is making concrete that grows its own moss
lead.summary: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Most building materials are designed to resist the elements, to stay sealed and unchanged for as long as possible. Respyre , a Dutch startup, is working from the opposite premise. The company has developed Mosscrete , a bioreceptive concrete coating that creates conditions for moss to grow directly on vertical surfaces, drawing moisture from rain and air without any soil or irrigation system. The science comes from research at Delft University of Technology , and since its commercial launch, Respyre has applied the technology across eight projects in Belgium and the Netherlands. How moss takes hold Moss doesn’t have roots in the conventional sense; it attaches to surfaces through rhizoids, tiny thread-like structures that cling to the material without penetrating or damaging it. Unlike a traditional green wall , which needs structural support for soil, a built-in watering system, and regular upkeep, Mosscrete sidesteps most of that. And because it’s applied as a coating rather than built in, it can go onto an existing facade just as easily as a new one. The material works especially well on blank or inaccessible walls where conventional planting isn’t an option, and Respyre has been using those spaces to test how the technology holds up under different real-world conditions. Eight buildings, different tests In Kortrijk, Belgium, 450 square meters (about 4,840 square feet) of a new industrial warehouse facade were coated with Mosscrete during construction and integrated with rainwater harvesting, keeping the whole system maintenance-free from day one. headline_hi: बंद होने पर भी खुली लाइब्रेरी
summary_en: There is lovely news related to education and books from Minnesota, USA. Here, the library in the town of Wyoming has started a new facility. This facility has been named 'Extended Access'. Under this, people can go inside even after the library closes. Readers can use computers even when no staff is present there. Local resident Michael Sayen often comes here to work on his days off. Sitting in this quiet place, he works on his novels and important documents. Library director Carla Lydon says this is very useful. Due to busy work hours, many people cannot come during the day. Now, such people can read at any time according to their convenience. Such arrangements are also starting in other states like California and Utah. This initiative is continuously expanding the reach of knowledge in rural areas.

lead.title: The Library Is Closed. Feel Free to Come In.
lead.summary: This story was originally published in the Daily Yonder. For more rural reporting and small-town stories visit dailyyonder.com . For Michael Sayen, visiting the local library after hours is a great way to get work done, or seek respite from the weather, regardless of what day it is. “We just had Labor Day, the library is closed all day. But if you have extended hours, you can come in and do the work, or cool down from a hot day or whatever you need to do,” Sayen said the day after Labor Day while working on a novel at the Wyoming, Minnesota branch of the East Central Regional Library (ECRL) in Chisago County. Sayen, who lives in nearby Forest Lake north of Minneapolis, adds that he has found after-hours access useful for filing time-sensitive job applications or court documents. Michael Sayen uses a computer at the Wyoming Giese Memorial Library to work on a novel. Sayen is a user of the Extended Access program at the Wyoming Library. Credit: H. Jiahong Pan/Daily Yonder The Wyoming branch library is home to a new ECRL initiative called “extended access,” which allows users to access a library branch when it is unstaffed. “We hope that it allows more people to use the facility, in particular those who may not be able to get to the library during otherwise limited hours due to work and family schedules,” ECRL executive director Carla Lydon wrote in an email. ECRL is one of a handful of rural library systems across the United States to offer such a service, increasing library access at a time when libraries are struggling for funding. How it works Extended access goes by many names depending on location. The Summit County Library in Utah calls it extended access hours . headline_hi: अल्पना कला से खुशियां बांटती दादी
headline_en: Grandmother spreading joy through Alpana art
summary_en: A very beautiful and heartwarming story has emerged from Kolkata. Here, seventy-four-year-old Ratnabali Ghosh wakes up at five-thirty in the morning. She creates traditional Bengali Alpana on the streets of Kolkata and outside people's doors. This initiative of hers started to surprise people and brighten their day. Now, it has become a beautiful mission to save Bengal's cultural heritage. She is spreading joy with her art among old houses, elderly couples, and residents of slums. Ratnabali ji is inspired by her grandmother and the artistic legacy of Rabindranath Tagore. She wants to revive this old tradition and pass it on to the new generation. Her effort teaches that along with modernity, preserving our roots is also very important. Truly, traditions are preserved through the desire to bring a smile to someone's face.

lead.title: This 74 Year Old Woman Is Bringing Alpona Art Back to Kolkata
lead.summary: At 74, Ratnabali Ghosh wakes up at 5:30 AM to bring smiles to Kolkata’s streets, one Alpona at a time! Known for creating traditional Bengali Alpona designs outside doorsteps, she began with a simple idea: surprise people and brighten their day. What started as a small initiative has grown into a beautiful mission to preserve Bengal’s cultural heritage. From decorating dilapidated houses to bringing joy to elderly couples and slum residents, her art reminds us that beauty and kindness belong everywhere. Inspired by her grandmother and Rabindranath Tagore’s artistic legacy, Ratnabali hopes to revive a fading Bengali tradition and pass it on to future generations. Her story carries a powerful message: modernisation matters, but our cultural roots deserve to be cherished, too. Sometimes, preserving a tradition begins with one person, a little creativity and the desire to make someone smile. Do you think traditional Indian art deserves more space in our modern cities?
